items.stem: Distinguish between error of omission and error of commission on the basis of example, meaning and effect on trial balance.
items.answer: (i) Example: error of omission: a credit purchase not recorded at all; error of commission: a credit sale to A debited to B. (ii) Meaning: error of omission: a transaction is wholly or partly left out; error of commission: a transaction is recorded wrongly (wrong amount, account or total). (iii) Effect on trial balance: error of omission: complete omission does not affect it; partial omission does; error of commission: some (wrong casting, wrong posting of amount) affect it; others do not.

items.stem: Explain any six steps to locate errors when the trial balance does not agree.
items.answer: (i) Recheck the totals of the trial balance: Re-add both columns. (ii) Check that every ledger balance is included: Compare the list of accounts with the ledger. (iii) Check the balancing of each account: Re-calculate balances, especially cash and personal accounts. (iv) Check the totals of subsidiary books: Recast the purchases, sales and returns books. (v) Divide the difference by 2: A balance put on the wrong side causes a difference of double its amount. (vi) Divide the difference by 9: If divisible, a transposition of digits (e.g. 54 as 45) is likely.
items.markingKey: Any six points, 1 mark each (heading and explanation): (i) Recheck the totals of the trial balance: Re-add both columns. (ii) Check that every ledger balance is included: Compare the list of accounts with the ledger. (iii) Check the balancing of each account: Re-calculate balances, especially cash and personal accounts. (iv) Check the totals of subsidiary books: Recast the purchases, sales and returns books. (v) Divide the difference by 2: A balance put on the wrong side causes a difference of double its amount. (vi) Divide the difference by 9: If divisible, a transposition of digits (e.g. 54 as 45) is likely.
